It is also delivered as methanol-ready for later conversion to methanol operation if required. Additionally, Everllence recently announced the 175DF-M, a high-speed, dual-fuel variant designed to operate on both diesel and methanol from the outset, with first customer deliveries planned for 2027.

title: Greek shipowners put Brussels on the spot over IMO deadlock
summary: Greek shipowners sharply criticize the EU for prioritizing its regional carbon regulations and associated revenue over a critical global IMO emissions agreement. This political deadlock risks stalling meaningful progress on carbon intensity, allowing high-emitting vessels to operate without robust international oversight. While policymakers squabble, the industry's dirtiest ships continue to burn fossil fuels, unhindered by effective, unified global standards.
content:
Greek shipowners have launched a fresh attack on Brussels ahead of the next round of international shipping emissions negotiations, accusing the European Union of putting its own regulatory interests ahead of a global agreement.

Union of Greek Shipowners president Melina Travlos warned on Monday that the EU’s unwillingness to compromise risks pushing the International Maritime Organization into another deadlock when talks resume in London next week.

Travlos said there had been no meaningful progress since the previous negotiating round in September and questioned whether Brussels was more interested in preserving its regional carbon regulations and the revenue they generate than securing a worldwide deal.

Greece and three other EU member states, together controlling around 70% of Europe’s shipping fleet according to Travlos, have repeatedly called for greater flexibility in the European negotiating position.

Those appeals, she said, had gone unanswered.

The intervention comes ahead of a November 23–27 IMO working group meeting, followed by the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s 85th session from November 30 to December 3. A further extraordinary session has been scheduled provisionally for December 4, subject to confirmation.

The talks will revisit the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, which combines a global marine fuel standard with an emissions-pricing mechanism. The negotiations have been held up by disagreements over the design, cost and implementation of the measures.

Travlos called for a framework reflecting the availability and cost of alternative fuels, the readiness of supporting infrastructure and competition for new fuels from other industries.

She also argued that energy-efficiency improvements and operational measures must remain part of the emissions-reduction toolkit rather than placing almost all the emphasis on alternative fuels.

Greek owners have long favoured a single international regulatory regime over overlapping regional requirements. The latest statement sharpens that position by directly questioning the EU’s negotiating intentions just days before governments return to London.

title: IMO faces challenges in net-zero framework compliance without emissions cost
summary: The IMO's "net-zero" framework faces critical delays, with member states failing to agree on crucial financial penalties for excessive emissions. The US leads opposition to a global carbon tax, effectively gutting incentives for shipping lines to abandon cheap, high-carbon fuels. Without mandatory financial consequences, claims of "decarbonization" remain mere greenwashing, as operators will predictably avoid more expensive, cleaner alternatives.
content:
Countries are struggling to design rules to make shipping companies comply with a new bunker regulation designed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, a senior International Bunker Industry Association official said Nov. 12, as Washington leads opposition to financial punitive measures.

International Maritime Organization member states, having failed to adopt the Net-Zero Framework as scheduled in October 2025, are due to meet again between Nov. 23 and Dec. 4 to discuss the regulation.

“People recognize that we need a GHG intensity marine fuel standard, and that is sort of generally agreed,” Edmund Hughes, IBIA’s representative to the UN agency, told Platts. “The sticking point is on the financial aspects.”

In its current form, the framework is composed of GHG intensity thresholds for marine energy that tighten progressively over 2028-2035, and financial costs for shipping companies failing to meet the standards.

But the US has fiercely opposed what it describes as “a global carbon tax” on shipping for the financial element, and a growing number of member states have proposed various revisions to the framework in bids to achieve a compromise.

“That is where we have the trouble. Because, obviously, the member states haven’t been able to identify the best approach,” Hughes said on the sidelines of the IBIA Annual Convention 2026.

Compliance mechanism

Countries supporting the current net-zero framework have designed the financial element to promote the use of low-carbon marine fuels, which remain much more costly than conventional, oil-based fuels due to limited availability.

October’s average delivered bunker costs for 0.5%-sulfur fuel oil are $22.78 per gigajoule in Singapore, compared with $27/GJ for bioblend B24, $28.48/GJ for LNG, and $48.47/GJ for 100% sustainable methanol, according to the Platts global bunker cost calculator.

“No shipping company is going to carry on buying more expensive fuel while their competitors are not,” Hughes said. “You need some way of closing that price gap.”

The IBIA official said challenges lie ahead for member states on how to design an alternative compliance mechanism if the current net-zero framework is to be revised.

Most Pacific Island states and EU member states are officially still supporting the current net-zero framework while the US and Middle Eastern states remain opposed to it. Japan, China, Norway and some major flag states have presented new ideas on compliance mechanisms.

“If you have a technical standard, you have to find a way to comply with it,” Hughes said. “You can go through quite a few semantic gymnastics to try and get the agreement, and that’s often what’s done at international level in multilateral discussions.”

Outlook

IBIA, the world’s largest trade association representing bunker industry participants, including bunker traders and fuel suppliers, has been granted consultative status with the IMO and its representatives regularly participate in IMO meetings.

“We recognize and value, as a sector, having global rules,” Hughes said. “That helps in all sorts of aspects in terms of understanding what the compliance requirements are, understanding what the market needs, what we need to provide in terms of fuels, and what people want to buy.”

Going forward, Hughes said IMO member states may need to coalesce around a net-zero framework in a return to its tradition of consensus building so future implementation could be ensured globally.

In April 2025, a total of 63 countries won a vote to approve the framework’s current text after the US withdrew from the negotiations. Later, 57 countries won another vote to delay its adoption in October 2025.

title: The Week in Alt Fuels: A drop in the tank
summary: Despite "alternative" fuel announcements, current small-scale projects offer negligible volumes against shipping's immense demand. Facilities producing just 1,000 to 10,000 tonnes of e-methanol annually represent mere drops compared to the thousands of tonnes a single vessel consumes. This insufficient progress guarantees continued reliance on high-carbon HFO, making FuelEU Maritime compliance and improved carbon intensity ratings an industry-wide challenge.
content:
Several producers are developing small-scale low- and zero-emission fuel projects around the world. But shipping needs far greater volumes available at competitive prices and at major bunker locations.

Several small-scale biofuel and e-fuel projects are being developed around the world.

Swiss startup Synhelion expects to start commercial operations at its 1,000 mt/year synthetic fuel plant in Germany in 2028. German-Brazilian startup Atlanteo is developing a modular e-methanol production concept, with its first 20 MW plant expected to produce around 10,000 mt/year.

European Energy’s Kassø e-methanol facility in Aabenraa, Denmark, which is already operating, produced 4,974 mt of e-methanol in the first half of 2026, against a planned capacity of 32,000 mt/year. The company is also planning a 48,000 mt/year e-methanol plant in Québec, Canada, with Greenfield Global.

ENGIE is planning a biomethane production facility at the HAROPA port complex in France, with an expected output of 7,000 mt/year intended for CMA CGM’s LNG-capable fleet.

Smaller-capacity projects can help developers test technologies, identify production challenges and establish commercial supply chains. But proving a concept works is one thing. Making it work at scale to meet potential demand is another.

A large ocean-going vessel can consume thousands of mt/year of fuel. That puts the output of a 1,000 mt/year plant into perspective. Even a 10,000 mt/year facility could typically serve only a limited number of vessels, depending on their size and fuel consumption.

And shipping is hardly the only customer waiting at the door. A number of low- and zero-emission fuel producers are diversifying the allocations across multiple sectors, including aviation, road transport, chemicals and fertilisers, leaving several industries competing for the same molecules.

Then comes the cost of getting that fuel to ships.

Producing renewable fuel at a competitive price doesn’t automatically make it a viable marine fuel option. Transport, storage and physical delivery costs can push up the final bunker price, particularly when production facilities are located far from major bunkering ports.

Longer transport distances could also increase associated emissions, potentially reducing the environmental benefits of switching to cleaner fuels.

This is where the distinction between scaling production and scaling supply becomes important.

Some developers intend to expand existing facilities, while others are pursuing networks of smaller plants.

Atlanteo, for instance, plans to replicate its modular facilities in locations with suitable renewable energy and agricultural resources. Synhelion has outlined plans for larger plants in Germany and Morocco.

Both approaches could increase production capacity. But the real commercial test is whether that fuel can reach ocean-going vessels in sufficient quantities without logistics costs undermining its appeal.

None of this diminishes the importance of smaller projects. They provide an opportunity to test technologies and work through practical challenges before committing to larger investments.

But a successful pilot is only the beginning.

For renewable fuels to make a meaningful contribution to deep-sea shipping, producers must eventually develop supply chains capable of delivering sufficient volumes at workable prices to the ports where vessels actually bunker.

In other alt fuels news this week, Frontier Fuels has chartered a barge for B100 deliveries on the Elbe, for supplying ships at five ports, including Hamburg and Cuxhaven. The barge, Lina, will carry only B100 (100% biofuel), the company said. It will also deliver to ships in Stade, Kiel and Brunsbüttel.

The VO Chidambaranar (VOC) Port Authority will commence methanol bunkering at the port by the end of November. The port’s methanol bunker infrastructure comprises an onshore storage facility connected to a jetty through a 2.8-km pipeline for shore-to-ship fuel transfers.

US LNG bunker supplier REV LNG completed an LNG bunkering operation for Siem Car Carriers’ vessel Aristotle, marking the first such operation at the Port of Davisville in Rhode Island. The truck-to-ship operation also marks the first LNG fuelling of a car carrier in the US Northeast, according to REV LNG.

title: Shipping sector backs an International Maritime Organization (IMO) climate deal, but not all of the details
summary: Major shipping companies and their associations publicly endorse an IMO climate deal, but their "support" hinges on weakening critical components. Industry players are actively pushing for softer carbon pricing, diluted fuel standards, and favorable emissions accounting, avoiding specific commitments post-postponement. This predictable maneuver risks another toothless IMO agreement, ensuring continued excessive HFO usage and further delaying genuine decarbonization efforts.
content:
New analysis from the global think tank InfluenceMap confirms, with detailed evidence, broad public support across the shipping and fuels sectors for a climate deal at the International Maritime Organization (IMO). However, differing advocacy positions on key components of the framework, including the carbon price, fuel standard, and rules for counting fuel emissions, threaten to weaken the proposed framework as negotiations resume this month, ahead of MEPC 85 (from 30 November) and the resumed adoption session on 4 December.

InfluenceMap identified high-level support for the IMO Net Zero Framework (NZF) from 13 companies and industry associations. Companies and industry associations alike have emphasized the need for a global framework to provide regulatory certainty for the industry’s energy transition, and reaffirmed their support for the IMO as global regulator. The International Chamber of Shipping (ICS), which represents over 80% of the world’s merchant fleet, and the World Shipping Council (WSC), which represents 90% of global liner shipping capacity, in 2025 urged governments to adopt the NZF as a “carefully balanced regulatory package”. European Shipowners (ECSA) has called global regulation essential “to deliver the energy transition of international shipping.” Other companies and associations that have shown support include CMA CGM, COSCO Shipping, Hapag-Lloyd, Moller-Maersk, Mediterranean Shipping Company, FuelsEurope, Ipieca, Renewable Fuels Association, Shell, and SEA-LNG.

However, in the past year, industry’s support for the Net-Zero Framework has become more cautious. Since adoption was postponed in October 2025, the main shipping associations, including the ICS and WSC, have avoided naming the framework, instead asking governments to “consider all options.” They have not proposed specific changes, but this softer messaging leaves room for a weaker deal. A significant risk remains that the IMO will deliver an agreement that undermines the global shipping industry’s ability to decarbonize, with less ambitious proposals creating a landing zone that moves the IMO away from the net-zero trajectory it agreed to in its 2023 GHG Strategy: net-zero emissions by or around 2050, with cuts of at least 20% by 2030 and 70% by 2040.

The NZF has two linked parts, a fuel standard that tightens over time and a carbon price on ships that miss it, both resting on life-cycle rules for counting each fuel’s emissions. InfluenceMap found engagement on these key elements from 4 industry associations: ICS, WSC, Ipieca and SEA-LNG. WSC supported all three elements. ICS broadly supported a carbon price but pushed for a weaker fuel standard ahead of the NZF’s approval in April 2025. Since then, Ipieca and SEA-LNG, representing oil and gas and LNG fuel interests, have advocated against strict GHG life-cycle rules.

Carbon Pricing: ICS and WSC both backed a carbon price, but ICS argued for a low and narrow one. Ahead of the NZF’s approval in April 2025, ICS proposed a carbon price of USD 10–20 per tonne of CO2e, charged only on emissions from burning fuel, not from producing it. WSC backed a carbon price set high enough to make clean fuels competitive, illustrated at USD 74 per tonne in 2030. Both organizations have had limited public positioning on the policy since April 2025.

Fuel Standard: WSC backed an ambitious standard; ICS argued for a weaker one. In 2024-25, ICS backed a fuel standard but proposed a 30% cut in fuel GHG intensity by 2040, less than half the 65% in the approved NZF. WSC supported the IMO’s fuel standard and its GHG intensity targets. Both organizations have had limited public positioning on the policy since April 2025. SEA-LNG opposed proposals that fuels should meet a minimum GHG threshold to count towards the standard.

Accounting Rules: Ipieca and SEA-LNG pushed to lower fossil fuels’ counted emissions; WSC backed stricter accounting. Since April 2025, Ipieca has advocated for replacing the IMO’s cautious default values for fossil fuels with averages and letting certificates stand in for clean power. SEA-LNG argued that LNG’s production emissions are lower than regulators assume. Both would make it easier for LNG-powered ships to comply.

The sharpest divide is between sectors. Shipping associations have broadly backed the framework’s core elements. Meanwhile, oil and gas sector groups have publicly supported the NZF while pushing at the IMO for accounting rules that would make fossil fuels, particularly LNG, count as cleaner. These rules decide how strict the framework is in practice, so loosening them could weaken it without changing the headline targets. The accounting rules are on the agenda when the IMO’s working group meets on 23–27 November.

Notably, InfluenceMap’s research found that support for the NZF often comes at the expense of regional regulations currently in force. ICS, WSC, SEA-LNG, and European Shipowners (ECSA) have leveraged support for a global framework to advocate against the FuelEU Maritime regulation and the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), calling for the review, harmonization, or withdrawal of these EU-level regulations following the passage of the IMO NZF, despite these rules already being in force and central to meeting EU climate targets.

title: Charting the Course: How to Navigate Maritime Shipping
summary: While the shipping industry focuses on navigating geopolitical disruptions and port congestion, there's a glaring omission of any strategy to mitigate the environmental impact of these challenges. Extended voyages due to Red Sea instability and Strait of Hormuz threats directly translate to higher fuel consumption, exacerbating carbon emissions from the fleet, particularly from HFO-burning ships. Industry solutions like 'carrier alliances' and 'digitization' are mere operational bandages, offering no credible plan to address the inevitable surge in carbon intensity and FuelEU Maritime compliance risks from these longer routes.
content:
Between shifting trade policies, geopolitical hot spots, port congestion, and rising regulations, ocean shipping is anything but smooth sailing. By leveraging carrier alliances and technology innovations, and implementing smart booking strategies, shippers can stay on course.

Maritime shipping, while never easy, has become even more difficult. “Ocean carriers and shippers are navigating geopolitical disruption, shifting trade policies, port congestion, weather-related impacts, and the need for more predictable service across global trade lanes,” says Claudia Kattan, vice president, logistics, for Central America, Mexico and Panama with Crowley, a maritime, energy, and logistics solutions company.

However, ocean carriers are working in multiple ways to boost their own resilience and reliability, including by forming alliances and investing in digitization. Shippers also can take steps to work more productively with carriers by developing a broad network of partner relationships and extending booking times, among other actions.

Geopolitical Tension Creates Challenges

Each year, ships move about 280 million containers across the world’s oceans, transporting roughly 80% of international trade when measured by volume, according to the World Shipping Council.

The most immediate disrupter to these journeys is geopolitical route instability, says Michael Augustin, principal director and ocean freight lead with Accenture. This instability impacts lead times, inventory buffers, supplier allocation, and network design. Both carriers and shippers now plan around the increasingly frequent geopolitical disruptions, rather than wait them out.

In the Red Sea, the Houthis have seized several islands, boosting their ability to control this important shipping route. Transit through the Suez Canal, which connects the Mediterranean and Red Seas, remains about 70% below 2023 levels.

The threat of confrontation in the Strait of Hormuz has prompted a 95% drop in traffic. Many ships now are diverting around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa.

The Panama Canal has become another pressure point, says Ian Wilson, principal analyst with Everstream Analytics. In late summer 2026, the Panama Canal Authority announced restrictions to the number of vessels that can move through the canal, citing a lack of rainfall and lower watershed inflows, as well as the forecast of a severe El Niño event.

Together, these challenges have depressed global shipping schedule reliability to around 56%, says Melissa Curry, vice president of global at NFI. They also lead to congested ports and localized shortages of specialized equipment, such as refrigerated trailers.

Because of the disruptions, carriers often need to balance excess capacity in some parts of their networks, with strained capacity elsewhere, says Priya Anand, director of global logistics services with Jabil, a provider of engineering, supply chain, and manufacturing solutions. At times, carriers have canceled scheduled voyages, which can artificially boost demand.

Spot rates are also up, often dramatically. The Shanghai-Los Angeles spot rate jumped 185% between September 2025 and September 2026, according to Wayfindr, a logistics provider. Similarly, the spot rate for the Shanghai-New York route was up 161% over the same period, Wayfindr says.

Carrier disruptions are particularly difficult because they rarely affect only the ocean legs of shipper supply chains, says Michael Britton, head of North America market, ocean products, with Maersk.

When vessels are rerouted or schedules change, the effects often ripple through transportation, warehousing, inventory planning, and other operations. For instance, shippers may boost inventory levels to ensure they have enough to cover the extended lead times.

Tariffs Have an Impact

At the same time, ongoing shifts in tariff policy make costs and demand patterns hard to predict, Augustin says. Shippers often accelerate purchases ahead of anticipated tariff deadlines, creating artificial spikes in volume that are then followed by aggressive pullbacks. These swings impact carriers’ revenue and complicate their network planning. They also upend shippers’ ability to plan.

As manufacturers have diversified at least some operations from China to other parts of the world, they’ve also generated new logistics requirements around ports, customs capabilities, lead times and other functions.

“Sourcing footprints are changing faster than transportation networks and infrastructure can adapt,” Augustin says. This often sparks capacity mismatches.

Another challenge is the “compounding event phenomenon,” Wilson says. When multiple disruptions hit at about the same time, the impact of each is magnified. For instance, Typhoon Saudel hit areas of China a few weeks after Typhoon Dolphin. Some port operators hadn’t cleared congestion from Dolphin before Saudel hit, making the jobs even more difficult.

Expanding regulations are also driving up shipping costs. For example, beginning in January 2026, the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) required ocean carriers to cover 100% of applicable emissions to, from, and within the EU. This effectively adds $50 to $100 per metric ton to fuel costs on European routes.

FuelEU Maritime further penalizes vessels using conventional fuels. While carriers are investing in LNG, methanol, and ammonia-ready vessels, their investments also drive up costs. “This is a structural freight cost floor that shippers need to budget for, independent of whatever rate volatility the market delivers,” Augustin says.

Best Thing Since Water

While the challenges are daunting, carriers are taking multiple steps to address them. A key one is the formation of global alliances between carriers (see box for more information). Through the alliances, the carriers remain competitors but share vessel space.

Maersk has indicated that one such alliance, The East-West Network, is “the best thing to happen to shipping since water.” This network is made possible by Gemini Cooperation, the name given to the collaboration between Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd. Gemini achieved schedule reliability above 90%, according to Hapag-Lloyd.

When individual routes are disrupted, carriers that operate within a coordinated alliance often have more flexibility to redeploy capacity, consolidate sailings, and protect schedule integrity than do carriers operating independently.

The alliances aren’t a panacea. Taking a hub-and-spoke approach, as many alliances do, can boost schedule reliability, but it can mean the cargo will take a more circuitous journey and require transshipping, says Guillaume Bournisien, managing director, freight forwarding, USA and Canada, with GEODIS.

The concentration of carriers can also lead to fewer independent options on major trade lanes, reducing shippers’ leverage in negotiations.

In addition, data standardization between ocean carriers is currently a question mark, Anand says. As a result, data may work differently, even between carriers within the same network. Shippers then need to create models to standardize the data so it is useful in decision-making.

The Digital Container Shipping Association (DCSA) does offer a reference page that shows which carriers have adopted which standards, says Lauren Beagen, chief executive officer and founder of The Maritime Professor.

In addition to forming alliances, some carriers are boosting regional connectivity. Crowley, for instance, recently added a weekly express service connecting Port Houston with markets in Guatemala and Honduras. This will help customers move goods efficiently across the Central America, U.S. and Caribbean trade lanes, with fewer handoffs, plus a broader equipment mix.

Digitization Takes Hold

As the “arteries of logistics” become increasingly fragile, and as more events disrupt planning, shippers need transparency. “Maritime is definitely the next industry that is up for an IT revolution,” says Karsten Schmidt, director of smart containers with Hapag-Lloyd. Information technology can provide this transparency.

Hapag-Lloyd is equipping its fleet of two million dry containers with Internet of Things (IoT) devices that frequently transmit location and condition updates. Shippers can leverage data from the devices, such as a container’s estimated arrival time at a warehouse, to enhance production and labor planning, Schmidt says.

Hapag-Lloyd also is working with ERP providers to ensure that data from the devices can be integrated within their systems.

The devices can be leveraged in other ways, as well. One company that works with raw materials plans to use the devices to reduce financing costs, Schmidt says, noting that a significant challenge in cargo financing is proving the cargo actually exists. An IoT tracker on a container can show this, as well as the cargo’s location. Having this information available may help companies reduce financing costs.

Another application of digitization, electronic bills of lading, could help mitigate cargo theft, as they’re generally less able to be modified than their paper counterparts, Beagen says. Across the industry, the adoption of electronic bills of lading could save $6.5 billion in direct costs, and enable up to $40 billion in global trade, according to a 2022 McKinsey study. However, not all countries currently have legal frameworks that formally acknowledge electronic bills of lading, the International Trade Centre notes.

While ocean carriers remain focused on the sea, many are adding services that can help shippers once their cargo reaches land.

Crowley, for instance, offers inland transportation, warehousing, and logistics services, Kattan says. Shippers can use the ocean service alone or add logistics support as market conditions, cargo requirements, and delivery timelines change.

Multiple carriers have been acquiring freight forwarding, customs brokerage, warehousing, and last-mile capabilities. If something does go wrong, shippers “have one throat to choke,” Augustin says.

On the other hand, the more bundled a relationship, the harder it is to switch out individual services or benchmark them against competitors’ offerings. Also, shippers’ negotiating leverage can erode over time.

Along with the actions that carriers are taking, shippers can do their part to work productively with their ocean transportation partners. A starting point is understanding how spiking fuel costs, additional surcharges, and other market shifts impact their own costs per unit, says Nick Bartlett, co-founder and director with Wayfindr.

Questions to ask include:

Should I ship?

Should I wait?

Should I front load?

Should I look at alternative fulfillment models?

Too Little, Too Late

Addressing these questions often requires some visibility into the carrier’s network. Without it, shippers often learn about variances, such as carriers canceling scheduled sailings or skipping planned port calls, perhaps to recover their schedules, too late to proactively adjust inventory, transportation, or customer commitments, Bournisien says.

The goal is to evaluate total costs of each carrier. A cheaper booking on a less-reliable carrier can end up costing more if it becomes necessary to add inventory because the schedule can’t be trusted.

“Shift the procurement lenses from price to reliability,” Bournisien says.

Building relationships with multiple ocean carriers and understanding the options they offer also helps when a shipper plans to enter new markets or consider new services. They’re not starting from zero, Beagen says.

Also, the deeper the carrier network that a shipper is using, the wider the benchmark for evaluating spot pricing. And while some shippers assume they lack leverage when negotiating with carriers, “everyone’s got leverage at some point,” Bartlett says, adding that shippers just need to know when to try to use it. For instance, if a vessel is rerouted with no notice, the carrier should face a penalty or other consequence.

Multiple Choice

Along with building a broad carrier network, shippers benefit by developing multiple options for different transportation modes, Anand says. If, for instance, ocean transport won’t move products as quickly as needed, a shipper might replace a segment of the trip with rail.

Given the current environment, Curry recommends shippers extend booking lead times to three to four weeks and build buffers of 10 to 14 days into their cargo-ready dates. And while shippers should maintain baseline cargo contracts for core stability, they’ll want to keep some portion of their volume flexible so they’re positioned to capitalize on potential post-peak rate adjustments and spot market capacity in late 2026.

Because the forces reshaping ocean freight, including geopolitical tension and shifting trade policies, are becoming structural in nature, ocean freight should no longer be managed in isolation. “It has become an integral component of sourcing, inventory and network strategy,” Augustin says.

Carrier-shipper relationships need to evolve into ones that are strategic, data-driven, and built around shared resilience.

Controlling Global Trade Routes

While individual cargo ships dominate the horizon, the real power on the water lies in shared networks. To maximize capacity and keep global trade moving, the world’s top ocean carriers pool their vessels into mega-alliances—or, in one notable case, leverage sheer size to chart a solo course (see sidebar). Here are the major players driving global shipping today.

OCEAN ALLIANCE

Primary Carriers: CMA CGM, COSCO, OOCL, Evergreen

Estimated Share of Global Capacity: Roughly 29%

Description: Massive capacity and broad networks; can run dense east-west networks

GEMINI COOPERATION

Primary Carriers: Maersk, Hapag-Lloyd

Estimated Share of Global Capacity: 21%

Description: Focus is on schedule reliability and operational stability through controlled connections

PREMIER ALLIANCE

Primary Carriers: ONE, HMM, Yang Ming

Estimated Share of Global Capacity: 18%

Description: Competitive on trans-Pacific and intra-Asian routes; network breadth and frequency through pooled capacity

INDEPENDENT

Carrier: MSC

Estimated Share of Global Capacity: 18%

Description: As an independent, can be less complex than an alliance

MSC Goes It Alone

While mega-alliances dominate much of container shipping, Mediterranean Shipping Co. (MSC) has charted a radically different course. Since August 2020, the Swiss carrier has acquired 500 secondhand ships, doubling its fleet capacity from 3.8 million to nearly 7.4 million TEU and capturing more than 21% of global liner capacity.

Combined with an aggressive newbuilding program, this rapid expansion propelled MSC past Maersk to become the world’s largest containerline. Crucially, that sheer fleet size has enabled a feat no major competitor has attempted: operating principal east-west trade lanes independently, without belonging to a global vessel-sharing alliance.

Following the conclusion of its 2M partnership with Maersk, MSC launched a standalone global network, demonstrating that unmatched scale can replace traditional partnership models.

title: IMO may codify alternative net-zero bunker rules in 2027: US FMC
summary: The IMO's "net-zero" bunker framework continues to drift, with final codification now optimistically slated for 2027, thanks to strong US opposition. The US Federal Maritime Commission rejects mandatory carbon bills, citing potential annual costs of $53 billion-$265 billion for the industry. This extended delay prioritizes financial concerns over immediate, tangible measures to reduce shipping's carbon intensity.
content:
The International Maritime Organization (IMO) may start forming consensus around an alternative Net-Zero Framework (NZF) in the coming weeks before hammering out its final text in 2027, US Federal Maritime Commission Chairman Laura DiBella said Nov. 11.

The UN agency is due to hold meetings Nov. 23-Dec. 4 to discuss the framework, after member states last year voted to delay its adoption by a year amid fierce US opposition.

“I hope we’re going to come to some sort of landing spot,” DiBella told Platts on the sidelines of the International Bunker Industry Association’s annual convention in New York City.

“I don’t think anything will be codified this year — maybe 2027, it will be codified. But I think we’ll come to some sort of consensus,” DiBella said.

The comments from the top US maritime regulator came after Japan, Panama, and some other countries proposed several alternatives to the NZF, which, in its current form, would place a mandatory cost on maritime greenhouse gas emissions from 2028 to promote a low-carbon bunker transition.

The US has estimated that the framework would cost the shipping industry $53 billion-$265 billion annually while arguing the incremental expenses would be ultimately passed on to businesses and consumers.

“We have the potential to take remedial action against the flag states that support it, that deliver cargo to the US,” DiBella said, referring to the FMC’s remit. “As the largest consumer of imported goods, we will face the biggest penalties. We don’t need additional inflationary measures on our cargo.”

But Washington would be open to what it believes to be a commercially realistic, technology-neutral NZF with achievable emissions targets, voluntary market-based compliance, and no mandatory carbon bills collected by the IMO, the US has suggested.

“The United States is working toward a consensus on something so that industry can make the necessary investments [in alternative fuels] and move ahead,” DiBella said.

Gas pathway

DiBella has displayed a favorable attitude toward LNG and bio-LNG and previously said in a web post that based on her personal view, the fuels could meet over 60% of global maritime bunker demand by 2050, and that the US is well positioned to supply the fuels as the world’s top LNG exporter, which could draw investments in increasing bio-LNG output with a “well-designed global fuel standard.

“The infrastructure is there to support it globally … I lean very heavy on the infrastructure side and what’s available and what’s realistic,” she told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy.
