title: Korean partnership’s carbon capture proposal selected as basis for IMO’s future safety guidelines
summary: The IMO has selected a Korean proposal as the foundation for future safety guidelines concerning onboard carbon capture systems (OCCS). This regulatory step, however, risks becoming a greenwashing distraction, offering distant technological promises instead of immediate, verifiable emission reductions. Real progress demands actual carbon intensity cuts today, not just frameworks for systems that may enable continued high-carbon fuel usage for vessels failing their CII ratings.
content:
A leading Korean public-private partnership comprising 10 maritime organizations has reached a major milestone in the development of international safety guidelines for onboard carbon capture and storage system (OCCS) after the proposal jointly developed by its members was selected as the base document for further development at the International Maritime Organization (IMO).

At the IMO’s 12th session of the Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers (CCC 12), the working group agreed to use the proposal from the Korean partnership as the basis for developing interim OCCS safety guidelines, incorporating elements of a separate proposal from the International Association of Classification Societies (IACS).

Established in April 2026, the partnership is led by Korea’s Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, with Korean Register (KR) overseeing regulatory development. Its members include HMM, Samsung Heavy Industries, Hanwha Ocean, HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering, Hyundai Heavy Industries Power Systems, HI Air Korea, PANASIA and the Korea Research Institute of Ships & Ocean Engineering (KRISO).

Drawing on the partners’ operational, shipbuilding, manufacturing and research expertise, KR consolidated their technical contributions into a single regulatory proposal, which was submitted to the IMO through the Ministry.

CCC 12 also agreed to establish the Correspondence Group on GHG Safety under Korea’s coordination to advance the guidelines. Joonghun Kim from KR’s Convention & Legislation Service Team has been named coordinator of the group and will bring together contributions from IMO Member States and international organizations to develop common safety requirements, with technology-specific annexes to be considered if time permits. The group will report its progress to CCC 13 in 2027.

Kyung-bok Kim, Executive Vice President of KR, said: “The practical experience, knowledge and expertise of the entire 10-member partnership have led to an important milestone in the development of OCCS safety standards at an IMO level. Our next step is to bring contributions from Member States and international organizations together to develop workable safety requirements.

“By leading the development of OCCS standards, Korea is leading the charge in the global decarbonization of the maritime industry, helping to ensure that safe, workable OCCS solutions become a practical reality for vessels worldwide,” he added.

The proposal builds on Korea’s multi-year OCCS development work, including raising safety concerns about the location of onboard CO₂ storage tanks in 2023 and proposing initial safety guidelines in 2024.

It also draws on technical assessments and operational experience associated with HMM Mongla, which was fitted with an OCCS solution in 2024 as part of a joint project involving HMM, Samsung Heavy Industries, PANASIA and KR. Ongoing risk assessments based on the vessel’s OCCS design identified 64 hazard scenarios, helping to inform the development of practical shipboard safety requirements.

The proposed guidelines address how OCCS equipment can be safely integrated with a vessel’s structure, layout and machinery systems. They cover practical safety considerations including CO₂ handling and storage, leakage prevention, emergency response and the safe transfer of captured carbon ashore. These requirements are intended to address not only the capture equipment itself, but also its interaction with other onboard systems and day-to-day vessel operations.

The framework retains a technology-neutral main body covering common safety requirements, alongside separate annexes addressing hazards specific to different OCCS technologies. This approach allows different capture methods, including chemical absorption, membrane separation and mineralization, to be considered without favoring a particular technology, while enabling requirements to evolve as further evidence becomes available.

Speaking about the importance of reflecting real-world operational experience in the proposed guidelines, members of the Korean partnership highlighted the need for practical standards that reflect the realities of running OCCS systems at sea.

Youngsun Kim, Senior Vice President, Director of Technology & Innovation Institute, HMM Co., Ltd., said: “Shipowners need standards covering safe operation, maintenance and offloading, not capture performance alone. It was important to be able to reflect actual operating conditions from an early stage of international guideline development.”

Ho-ki Lee, Vice President at Samsung Heavy Industries, said: “At CCC 12, we saw growing consensus around onboard carbon capture as a practical option for decarbonizing shipping. Drawing on our experience in shipbuilding and OCCS demonstration, we will contribute to international safety guidelines that enable carbon capture systems to operate safely and efficiently on board ships.”

Yoon-Sik Hwang, Vice President at Hanwha Ocean, said: “This joint proposal is particularly meaningful because it brings together expertise from shipbuilding, shipping, marine equipment and classification. Hanwha Ocean will continue contributing to the development of international safety guidelines, drawing on its demonstration experience and technical capabilities to accelerate the commercialization of onboard carbon capture technology.”

Sangmin Park, Senior Vice President at HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering, said: “The acceptance of the Korean-led proposal on interim OCCS safety guidelines is a meaningful achievement towards the commercialization of onboard carbon capture technology. Drawing on the experience accumulated through OCCS technology development, HDKSOE will contribute to international safety guidelines to support the safe application of OCCS on ships.”

Jeongsu Seo, Executive Director at HI AIR KOREA, said: “Safety functions must be capable of being tested and verified in the field. Drawing on our experience in developing and demonstrating mineralization-based capture technology, we will contribute to practical safety standards for both newbuildings and retrofits by linking that experience to leak detection and emergency shutdown requirements.”

title: The Demand-Side Case: Scope 3 Pressure and Maritime Decarbonisation Gap
summary: The IMO's MEPC 83 again failed to implement a global $150-per-tonne CO₂ shipping levy, demonstrating its continued inability to enforce meaningful decarbonisation. However, corporate Scope 3 emissions targets are now forcing logistics providers to demand genuine carbon intensity data from their shipping partners. This external pressure, not bureaucratic talks, will expose which ships are still burning excessive HFO and exceeding their CII ratings.
content:
In April 2025, the International Maritime Organization's (IMO) 83rd Marine Environment Protection Committee meeting ended without consensus on a global shipping levy. The proposed Net Zero Fund (NZF), a $150-per-tonne charge on shipping CO₂ emissions projected to raise some $120 billion a year to fund further decarbonisation projects, remains unagreed for now.

The noise declared progress on maritime decarbonisation had stalled, but there is an underlying signal that tells a different story, with quiet progress in procurement departments from Stockholm to São Paulo to Seoul.

Corporate sustainability teams asked the same question of their logistics providers: what is the carbon intensity of the ship carrying my goods, and what are you doing to reduce it?

Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) commitments to reduce Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions were already operative. They just didn't need a UN agreement.

But what is that signal, and how strong is it? Here we quantify that signal and what it means for shipping markets, and why it matters now, even at a fraction of the NZF's scale

Scope 3: the new charter conversation

Scope 3 refers to indirect emissions from across a company's value chain, up and downstream of its own operations. They are the least visible and least actioned part of corporate climate commitments.

Scope 3 are also, on average, 26 times larger than a company's direct (Scope 1 and 2) emissions. For a fashion retailer, a pharmaceutical company, or an electronics manufacturer, the largest single component of Scope 3 is usually transportation, and that transportation usually includes shipping.

The GHG Protocol's Category 4 (upstream transportation and distribution) and Category 9 (downstream transportation) capture this exposure. Until recently, few companies reported on them with any rigour, fewer still tying targets to them.

That has changed. In September 2025, 8.8% of all companies (1,046 of the full SBTi database of 15,564 companies) included SBTi-validated near-term targets naming upstream transportation with the top sectors, food and beverage (152 companies), textiles and apparel (91), pharmaceuticals (89), and retail (70). These are, without exception, the largest volume shippers of containerised cargo on the planet.

And these are not soft commitments. SBTi validation requires targets to be consistent with 1.5°C or well-below 2°C pathways, independently reviewed, and publicly disclosed. If a major food group or a global apparel brand has an SBTi-validated Cat 4 target, it is legally and reputationally exposed if it cannot demonstrate progress. That exposure flows directly to the choice of carrier.

The fleet cannot yet deliver

So the demand for lower emission shipping is there, but there’s a problem. The fleet cannot absorb it.

The IMO's revised GHG Strategy requires international shipping to cut its carbon intensity by 40% from 2008 levels by 2030, dropping from a fleet average of approximately 100 grams of CO₂ per tonne-mile to around 72 by 2030. That 28% gap must be closed in less than four years, across 165,000 active vessels.

In the first year of Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) reporting in 2023, 30% of the active fleet attained the two lowest grades, D or E, which trigger improvement plans and, eventually, commercial consequences. That is roughly 49,500 ships.

The supply response is modest. Of those 165,000 active vessels, just 1.5% (2,493 vessels) could run on alternative fuels. Of the global orderbook of 10,355 vessels, by early 2024, only 14% of ordered new tonnage was alternative-fuel-ready (UNCTAD RMT 2024). At the current pace, replacing the D/E-rated fleet would take nearly five years, and most use conventional fuel.

A year ago that premium barely existed. Today it is a negotiating variable on every long-term charter. And clients with Scope 3 targets are ever more willing to pay it, or require it as a condition of contract.

Quantifying the pressure

We modelled three scenarios for how 1,046 Cat 4-committed companies translate into shipping market demand. The scenarios bracket the plausible range of shipper behaviour given different levels of procurement engagement.

Passive: the conservative floor

Five per cent of committed companies actively specify vessel performance in charter decisions. The rest report but do not act. At a shadow carbon price of $20 per tonne CO₂ equivalent, the implied annual demand signal on containerised trade is worth approximately $0.7 billion. This is the floor and already happening.

Active Procurement: the base case

Twenty-five per cent of committed companies specify eco-vessels, consistent with observed behaviour among Sea Cargo Charter signatories. After a 40% efficiency discount, accounting for vessel availability constraints and contract timing gaps, the implied signal on 2.335 billion tonnes of containerised trade, at a shadow price of $45 per tonne, is approximately $4.7 billion per year.

MBM / Book & Claim: the upside

An additional 10% engage via Book & Claim certificates or nascent maritime emissions trading mechanisms, adding to the Active scenario. After a 60% efficiency discount (the Book & Claim market for shipping is still thin), the combined signal reaches approximately $10.7 billion per year.

These are shadow carbon costs: the value shippers assign to emissions when choosing between vessels. No money changes hands, and there is no tax or surcharge but these numbers influence real chartering decisions. A shipper using a $45 carbon price and accepting a 10-12% eco-premium is making the same basic calculation as under a carbon levy, just on a voluntary basis.

What the NZF stalemate means

The IMO NZF is a supply-side mechanism that would change the economics for every ship at $150 per tonne of CO₂, raising $120 billion a year to find alternative fuel infrastructure in developing countries and de-risked newbuild orders at a scale that the market cannot achieve alone.

Scope 3 pressure is demand-side, working through very different levers, the shipper's procurement decision, the charter contract, the sustainability questionnaire, the annual CDP disclosure.

However, the Scope 3 signal covers only a fraction of seaborne trade, primarily containerised cargo where shipper brand exposure is highest. It seldom reaches bulk carriers where cargo owners rarely have a Scope 3 alignment incentive. Scope 3 incentives are uneven, voluntary, and unenforceable. When it eventually comes, NZF, will do things Scope 3 pressure structurally cannot.

But the SBTi commitment pipeline is growing at approximately 35% per year. The first wave of Cat 4 targets, set in 2021 and 2022, hit reporting deadlines in 2025 and 2026. Companies setting 30% reduction targets with a 2025 base year will be audited against those targets imminently. That creates a step-change in the urgency of Scope 3 procurement, independent of anything IMO does.

What Scope 3 means for shipowners and financiers

For shipowners, eco-efficient vessels now carry a demonstrable commercial premium, and that premium has a structural driver, the Scope 3 commitment pipeline, that will intensify over the next three years regardless of IMO outcomes. Vessels with verified emissions intensity data, GLEC-compliant reporting, and CII ratings of A or B will be the only choice for the committed shipper segment.

The 36 Poseidon Principles signatory banks represent some 75% of global ship finance and measure their portfolios' carbon alignment annually. An owner’s access to competitive financing increasingly depends on its emissions profile. The Scope 3 and Poseidon stories are converging: the shipper's charter choice and the bank's lending decision are shaped by the same underlying decarbonisation pressure.

For financiers, the 41% of the fleet aged 25 years or more represents the most acute risk. These vessels are unlikely to retrofit economically, many facing accelerating obsolescence as the charter market polarises between compliant and non-compliant tonnage.

The combination of CII D/E ratings, Poseidon Principles portfolio pressure, and shipper Scope 3 specification requirements creates a compounding stranded-asset risk for older tonnage not yet priced into most residual value curves.

title: Shipping's $95bn fossil fuel bonfire
summary: The shipping industry burned an estimated $95 billion on fossil fuels in just nine months, a direct consequence of its unsustainable dependence and volatile markets. This colossal sum, enough to finance widespread wind propulsion, was instead wasted, offering zero return on long-term energy security or emissions reduction. This continued reliance directly exacerbates carbon intensity metrics and guarantees increasing FuelEU Maritime fines, exposing the industry's failure to genuinely decarbonize.
content:
The shipping industry has spent an estimated $95bn more on fuel since the Hormuz crisis began. That money could have financed wind propulsion across much of the world’s merchant fleet, slashing emissions and reducing exposure to future energy shocks. Gavin Allwright, secretary-general of the International Windship Association (IWSA), writes for Splash today.

The maritime shipping industry just set $95bn on fire.

Over the past nine months, geopolitical turmoil around the Strait of Hormuz has forced the sector to absorb a massive fossil fuel premium. Had that exact capital been invested into free, zero-emission wind propulsion instead of pouring it into volatile oil markets, shipowners would already be saving billions while helping to permanently secure their energy independence.

As negotiators head to the International Maritime Organization (IMO) this December, they are drawing red lines over a proposed $11bn-$12bn fund for the Net-Zero Framework. Yet, the industry just handed over nearly eight times that amount to fossil fuel suppliers since late February. This shocking amount represents a massive transfer of wealth out of the maritime sector with absolutely zero return on long-term energy security or commercial resilience.

This is my maths. Since the beginning of this recent geopolitical instability, spiking fuel costs drained an extra $340m a day from the industry throughout March alone. With the global average price of Very Low Sulphur Fuel Oil (VLSFO) surging from $500 to $810 per tonne – with other fuels spiking even higher, making the monthly fuel bill skyrocket from $12.5bn to well over $20bn. If the numbers don’t lie, this adds up to a $95bn toll simply because the industry remains dependent on fossil fuels in an increasingly unstable world and extremely volatile markets.

That lost capital could have driven vessels’ energy independence instead. Wind propulsion harnesses a globally abundant energy source delivered entirely free at the point of use. For $95bn, between 100,000 and 200,000 wind-assist retrofit systems could have been funded. That is enough to equip half the current global fleet, slash fuel consumption by 5%, and eliminate 45m tonnes of CO2e emissions every single year.

Because wind energy is free, those immediate fuel savings would unlock a further $12bn annually, providing the exact capital needed to reinvest in up to 20,000 more systems a year. By 2040, this deployment cycle would have fully paid for itself, putting that initial $95bn back into shipowners’ pockets to fund further decarbonisation.

Alternatively, that same cash could have financed 5,000 to 10,000 newbuild primary-wind vessels, fundamentally transforming the sector by cutting fuel use and emissions by up to 80% per ship.

Additionally, this evaporated capital could have fully funded a just and equitable transition for the entire maritime workforce. It could have seamlessly financed the retraining of the 600,000 seafarers who will need to operate alternative technologies and new fuels by the mid-2030s. It would have easily covered the initial $300m-$500m needed by the Pacific Blue Shipping Partnership to deliver dozens of primary wind ships to Pacific islands. With $95bn, we could have scaled this further and rolled out similar programs globally, freeing the world’s most vulnerable economies from their expensive fossil fuel dependency.

We cannot recover the billions already burned, but we can stop the bleeding. The ongoing geopolitical crises have ruthlessly exposed the devastating cost of climate inaction and fossil fuel reliance. This December, the Net-Zero Framework is up for adoption once again at IMO and would catalyse the rapid scaling of wind technology and help break the cycle.

title: Onboard carbon capture: a practical pathway for shipping?
summary: While touted as a decarbonization 'pathway,' current onboard carbon capture (oCCS) systems for ships like Eastern Pacific Shipping's *Pacific Cobalt* capture a mere 30-40% of CO₂ emissions, with larger pilots aiming for 70%. Crucially, operating these systems demands 15-30% more fuel, directly increasing the vessel's gross carbon emissions and potentially pushing its carbon intensity (CII) rating into failing territory. Such inefficiency means a '70% capture' system with a 15% fuel penalty delivers only a 44% net CO₂ reduction, making it a costly greenwashing exercise rather than a serious solution to avoid FuelEU Maritime fines, particularly for HFO-burning vessels.
content:
From first installations to commercial use

Early commercial installations show oCCS moving beyond concept and pilot-scale development, with amine-based post-combustion capture emerging as the most mature marine option. This is currently the only technology with classed commercial installations, where full-scale systems capture around 30% to 40% of CO₂ emissions. Larger pilots target about 70%.

Eastern Pacific Shipping’s Pacific Cobalt became the first classed commercial oCCS installation in 2024 under LR’s Emission Abatement Carbon Capture & Storage (EACCS) (Amine, HFO) class notation, while Solvang’s Clipper Eris is testing a full-scale system designed to capture around 70% of the CO₂ produced by its main engine. These projects add to the growing evidence that oCCS can operate at commercial scale, but its wider value depends on the emissions reductions achieved in practice.

That depends partly on the energy needed to operate the system, which can increase fuel consumption by 15% to 30% in current applications. A 70% gross capture with a 15% fuel penalty would deliver an estimated tank-to-wake CO₂ reduction of around 44%, although waste-heat recovery could reduce that penalty. The resulting emissions reduction, cost and operational impact will vary between ships, making vessel suitability central to the business case.

Finding the right ships

Panos Mitrou, LR Senior Vice President of Shipping Strategy states: “Onboard carbon capture has the potential to become an important part of shipping's decarbonisation toolkit. For the right vessel types and trades, it offers a realistic pathway to reducing CO₂ emissions and managing carbon costs while fuel supply chains, infrastructure and regulations continue to evolve.”

The strongest opportunities for oCCS are likely to be those vessels with sufficient remaining trading life and space for the equipment. The business case will also depend on how and where these vessels operate. For example, medium range and chemical tankers trading on EEA routes have frequent port calls, offering opportunities to offload captured CO₂ while EU carbon-price exposure increases the value of reducing emissions.

For LNG-fuelled vessels and LNG carriers, cold energy released during LNG vaporisation can help liquefy captured CO₂, reducing additional power requirements. Short-sea and feeder vessels could also benefit from predictable routes and regular opportunities to offload. The case for oCCS therefore depends on the technology fitting a vessel’s operating and commercial conditions.

Without these or similar conditions, the case weakens. Ships with limited trading life, little carbon-price exposure or poor access to offloading facilities will be less likely to justify the investment. Access to offloading is another critical factor because onboard storage is limited, setting a limit on how long the system can operate before captured CO₂ must be removed. Voyage length and offloading opportunities therefore directly affect how much CO₂ can ultimately be captured, making where and how a vessel operates as important as what can be installed onboard.

The decisive challenge lies ashore

For oCCS to deliver its intended benefits, captured CO₂ must enter a transport and storage network leading to permanent storage or an eligible use. Limited port reception infrastructure is a constraint, with few ports able to receive ship-captured liquefied CO₂. Many existing facilities are designed for food-grade CO₂ that may not suit exhaust-derived streams. Development is furthest ahead in north-west Europe, supported by emerging North Sea transport and storage networks, but access remains limited elsewhere.

The emissions benefit must also be recognised within relevant regulatory frameworks. The EU ETS can recognise captured CO₂ that reaches qualifying permanent storage or utilisation, while FuelEU Maritime does not yet include oCCS in its greenhouse-gas intensity calculations. The IMO is still developing a global framework covering safety, testing, verification and carbon accounting. Practically, the success of oCCS depends on infrastructure and regulation developing alongside the technology.

title: Fund for Energy Efficiency Technologies (FEET) is the first fund to adopt the Singapore-Asia Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance
summary: A new "Fund for Energy Efficiency Technologies" (FEET) adopts Singapore's taxonomy, aiming to guide investments into vessel retrofits and incremental efficiency measures. While touting "verified fuel savings" and robust MRV, this initiative must prove it will genuinely slash carbon intensity, not merely prolong the operational life of the dirtiest ships. We remain skeptical if such funding truly prevents FuelEU Maritime fines or enables HFO-guzzling vessels to barely meet their ever-tightening CII ratings.
content:
The Fund for Energy Efficiency Technologies (FEET) has adopted the second edition of the Singapore-Asia Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance (SAT) to guide investment decisions, making FEET the first fund to adopt the SAT. The revised SAT criteria recognise qualifying vessel retrofits and energy efficiency technologies (EET) installations that deliver measurable greenhouse gas emissions reductions.

The Singapore Sustainable Finance Association (SSFA), supported by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), announced the second edition of the SAT at COP31 in Türkiye. At the launch event, FEET’s adoption of the revised taxonomy was highlighted as an example of how transition taxonomies can inform capital allocation in hard-to-abate sectors, where emissions reductions often require incremental investments in existing assets.

The Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) also announced that Lloyd’s Register (LR) has completed its independent review of the Centre’s methodology for quantifying fuel savings from WAPS, which underpins FEET’s financing of these projects.

Together, these developments reinforce the role of measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) to inform investment decisions in maritime decarbonisation, with the updated taxonomy providing a credible framework, and GCMD’s independently reviewed methodology specifying what evidence is needed and how to measure performance.

FEET is the world’s first fund to link verified fuel and regulatory savings from EETs installed on vessels to a pay-as-you-save mechanism. It offers up to 100% upfront financing through a blended finance structure. FEET is managed by AIM Horizon Investments, with GCMD as the fund’s decarbonisation advisor, and is supported by the Development Bank of Japan, DBS Bank and ING.

Experience from real-world pilots helped shape taxonomy update

SSFA engaged with the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) and GCMD to review how the SAT can be applied to EET retrofits and installations. Others involved include ING and DNV. GCMD drew on operational experience from its EET pilots to show how fuel savings can be quantified credibly under real-world conditions.

Fuel savings methodology independently reviewed

GCMD’s methodology to quantify fuel savings builds on its pilot with Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS) on board the MV Pacific Sentinel. During the pilot, GCMD collected 276 million data points over four months of spot-market trading in the Americas. From these, GCMD screened more than 3,000 on-off transitions and identified 203 in which operating conditions remained constant between the on and off states. This allowed fuel savings to be isolated and uniquely attributed to the wind sails, rather than changes in operating conditions.

LR’s independent review concluded that the methodology aligns with relevant industry standards and incorporates current best practices to assess WAPS performance.

Going forward, the methodology specifies how fuel savings will be determined for the WAPS projects FEET finances, with its assumptions, data collection and analyses contractually agreed among all parties. For each project, the data will be further audited, and the calculated fuel savings will be independently verified. These verified savings will then determine shipowners’ payments under the pay-as-you-save mechanism.

‘’Even small gains in fuel efficiency can deliver meaningful fuel cost savings over a vessel’s operating life, but financing them depends on confidence in the numbers. Trust in data is what accelerates adoption. By placing robust MRV at the heart of FEET, and now aligning it with the revised taxonomy and an independently reviewed methodology, we hope to give shipowners and financiers confidence to deploy these solutions.’’

Professor Lynn Loo, CEO, GCMD

‘’Measurement and independent verification of fuel and regulatory savings are crucial to reaching agreement on a pay-as-you-save financing mechanism with shipowners to which FEET provides financing of energy efficiency technologies. FEET’s own current providers of equity and debt capital welcome the adoption of the SAT by FEET and other such capital providers will show an interest in this approach to supporting maritime decarbonisation.’’

Marcel de Bruijckere, CEO, AIM Horizon Investments

title: Yacht sector must prepare for potential expansion of EU ETS
summary: The luxury yacht sector, historically prioritizing opulence over environmental responsibility, is now warned to prepare for potential EU ETS expansion. This isn't merely a "greenwashing" opportunity; the scheme directly links carbon costs to actual greenhouse gas emissions, penalizing inefficient vessels. Owners must finally confront their vessels' excessive fuel consumption and carbon intensity or face substantial financial penalties for every tonne of CO2 emitted.
content:
Understanding the implications

According to Engel-Jan de Boer, LR's Global Yacht Segment Director, the industry should use the current legislative process as an opportunity to assess the potential impact of carbon pricing rather than waiting for a final decision.

"While these proposals are still subject to political negotiation, maritime emissions are becoming subject to increasing scrutiny and the yacht sector should be monitoring these developments closely.

“We have seen in the past how parts of the industry were slow to react to major regulatory changes such as IMO Tier III emissions requirements and the Maritime Labour Convention. Those who engaged early were able to plan and adapt, while others were forced into reactive compliance programmes under significant time pressure.

“Owners, managers, designers and shipyards should therefore be considering the potential operational, technical and commercial implications now, even as the legislative process continues."

Why efficiency matters

Much of the discussion around EU ETS focuses on the potential increase in operating costs. However, de Boer believes the yacht industry should view the scheme through a different lens.

"The scheme is often viewed simply as a tax on fuel, but in reality it rewards efficiency," he says.

Because compliance costs are directly linked to greenhouse gas emissions, vessels that consume less fuel for a given operating profile will face lower carbon costs than less efficient counterparts.

That distinction is particularly relevant for the yacht sector. Unlike commercial shipping, where efficiency is often linked to cargo transport, yachts have traditionally been designed around criteria such as comfort, range, performance and guest experience. As environmental regulation evolves, energy efficiency is increasingly joining that list of design considerations.

Variations in hull form, onboard energy demand, operating profile and the use of technologies such as hybrid propulsion can all influence a vessel's emissions footprint. Under a carbon pricing regime, those differences could have a direct financial consequence.

Rewarding early adopters

Many of the technologies already gaining traction within the yacht sector could become more attractive as carbon costs become a longer-term operational consideration.

Hybrid propulsion systems, battery energy storage, shore power connectivity and advanced energy management systems can help reduce fuel consumption as well as emissions. At the same time, growing interest in fuel-flexible designs and alternative fuels reflects a wider shift towards improving overall energy performance.

Rather than driving a single technological solution, an expanded ETS framework would reinforce existing efforts to reduce fuel consumption and improve vessel efficiency. For owners and operators, the commercial value of energy-saving technologies may become easier to quantify if carbon costs become part of the operating equation.

title: India–South Korea Cooperation on Alternative Maritime Fuels and Port Energy Systems
summary: Despite talks of "alternative fuels," India and South Korea's maritime sectors collectively emitted over 44.8 million tonnes of CO₂e in 2022. While policymakers discuss hydrogen and ammonia, heavy fuel oil continues to power the vast majority of vessels, exposing the industry's slow transition. Real decarbonisation, driven by measures like FuelEU Maritime, demands immediate HFO phase-out, not just future port energy hubs.
content:
This article originally appeared in ‘Oceans of Alignment: India–South Korea Cooperation in the Indo-Pacific’

Maritime transport carries more than 80 percent of global merchandise trade by volume, making it the backbone of global supply chains.[1] At the same time, international shipping accounts for around 3 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, making it one of the most difficult sectors to decarbonise.[2] The International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) 2023 Revised Greenhouse Gas Strategy established a pathway towards net-zero emissions from international shipping by or around 2050, while regional measures such as the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU-ETS) and FuelEU Maritime are accelerating demand for cleaner fuels and lower-emission shipping operations. These policy shifts are reshaping competition across the maritime sector by linking shipping emissions to production of clean fuels and the availability of lowcarbon port infrastructure.

India and South Korea also face a growing domestic imperative to decarbonise their maritime sectors.

According to their respective submissions to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), India’s maritime activities, including international fleet bunkering, emitted over 6.4 million tonnes of CO₂e,[3] while South Korea’s domestic and international navigation emitted approximately 38.4 million tonnes of CO₂e in 2022.[4]

These developments indicate that maritime decarbonisation is no longer a question of improving vessel efficiency but increasingly depends on two interdependent energy value chains: the first centres on the production, storage and supply of low-carbon marine fuels, including green hydrogen, ammonia, and methanol; while the second focuses on transforming ports into energy hubs capable of electrifying port operations, supplying shore power, and supporting alternative fuel bunkering.

Alternative Maritime Fuels

Heavy fuel oil has powered global shipping for decades because of its high energy density and suitability for long-distance ocean transport.[7] However, the IMO’s decarbonisation pathway and emerging fuel regulations are accelerating interest in green ammonia and green methanol, both of which are increasingly viewed as leading candidates for deep-sea shipping.

Green ammonia has emerged as a leading long-term option for deep-sea shipping because it contains no carbon and offers notably higher volumetric energy density than hydrogen while avoiding the need for cryogenic or high-pressure storage systems.[8] Green methanol, by contrast, is easier to handle using existing fuel infrastructure but requires a sustainable carbon feedstock, which can be derived from captured CO₂ (e-methanol) or from biomass-derived carbon (bio-methanol), making large-scale production more complex despite its operational advantages.[9]

For ports, these fuels represent more than a decarbonisation pathway. Green hydrogen and its derivatives—like green ammonia and green methanol—can reduce emissions from port operations while creating entirely new revenue streams through fuel bunkering and exports.10 Realising this opportunity, however, will require new storage and transmission infrastructure, dedicated safety standards, large-scale in[10]vestment, and coordinated regulatory frameworks to enable ports to become integral nodes within the emerging green hydrogen economy and contribute to a broader energy transition.[11]

India’s comparative advantage lies upstream in producing these future maritime fuels. The National Green Hydrogen Mission identified Deendayal Port (Kandla), Paradip and V.O. Chidambaranar (Tuticorin) as Green Hydrogen Hubs to integrate renewable energy, hydrogen production, and maritime applications.[12] India’s competitive renewable energy costs have already translated into some of the world’s lowest discovered prices for green hydrogen and green ammonia, strengthening its prospects as a future exporter of zero-carbon maritime fuels.[13] This ambition is reinforced by the Harit Sagar-Green Port Guidelines, which require all major ports to establish green ammonia bunkering and refuelling facilities by 2035.[14]

There have been many noteworthy developments at the Deendayal Port Authority: in 2025, a 1-megawatt (MW) electrolyser-based green hydrogen plant was commissioned, while India’s first shore-to-ship methanol bunkering demonstration was completed in April 2026, and the port aims to supply around 500 kilo tonnes per annum (KTPA) of Renewable Fuels of Non-Biological Origin (RFNBO)-compliant e-methanol by 2028–29, with plans to scale hydrogen production to 10 MW.[15]

India has begun embedding this transition within its maritime strategy. With nearly 95 percent of the country’s trade by volume moving through sea routes, ports are strategic gateways for economic growth and international trade.5 The Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 thus positions green fuels, carbon-neutral ports, and maritime decarbonisation as strategic priorities aligned with the IMO’s net-zero agenda.

Similarly, South Korea has embedded maritime decarbonisation within its national policy framework. In 2026, the National Assembly passed the Green Shipping Corridor Support Act to accelerate low-emission shipping routes and support port infrastructure.6 Together with Korea’s leadership in shipbuilding, this legislation positions the country at the forefront of next-generation maritime technologies. It is home to three of the world’s largest shipbuilders—HD Hyundai, Hanwha Ocean, and Samsung Heavy Industries— and remains a global leader in the construction of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG)-, methanol-, and ammonia-capable vessels.

Against this backdrop, India and South Korea possess complementary capabilities across the emerging maritime energy ecosystem. India’s strengths lie in renewable energy deployment, emerging green fuel production capabilities, and expanding port infrastructure, whereas South Korea leads in advanced shipbuilding, alternative-fuel vessels, and smart port technologies. This article examines how India and South Korea can jointly build the infrastructure needed for maritime decarbonisation through two interconnected energy value chains: alternative maritime fuels and ports as integrated energy systems; to advance both bilateral cooperation and the broader transition towards resilient, low-carbon maritime networks across the Indo-Pacific.

The V.O. Chidambaranar (VOC) Port has emerged as India’s leading green maritime fuel hub, becoming the country’s first port to produce and utilise green hydrogen onsite while simultaneously developing green methanol and green ammonia bunkering infrastructure.[16] In 2026, AM Green and VOC Port signed an agreement to establish up to 200 KTPA of green ammonia bunkering capacity by 2029–30, positioning it as one of India’s first dedicated green ammonia bunkering hubs.[17]

Paradip Port, meanwhile, is developing a dedicated jetty and allied facilities capable of handling up to 4 million tonnes per annum (MTPA) of green hydrogen and green ammonia and other liquid cargo following approval by the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (MoPSW) in February 2026, establishing India’s eastern coast as an export gateway for future maritime fuels.[18]

Figure 1: Major Seaports of India and South Korea

Source: Maps of India and Ministry of Oceans and Fishers, Republic of Korea[19]

South Korea, in contrast, occupies the downstream end of the value chain. It has become a global leader in technologies compatible for utilising low-carbon maritime fuels. Korean shipbuilders are leading the development of ammonia-ready vessels, methanol-powered ships and dual-fuel propulsion systems, while ports such as Busan and Ulsan are developing commercial methanol and ammonia bunkering capabilities.

Busan has completed LNG and methanol ship-to-ship bunkering demonstrations and is preparing for commercial-scale deployment as demand for alternative marine fuels expands.[20]

Under South Korea’s Eco-friendly Fuel Supply Chain Development Strategy, Ulsan has been designated the national hub for LNG, methanol, and ammonia bunkering.[21] In April 2026, Ulsan Port completed the commercial pipe-to-ship (PTS) green ammonia bunkering operation, supplying 600 tonnes of green ammonia to an ammonia-fuelled vessel built by HD Hyundai Heavy Industries. This marked the world’s first commercial application of ammonia as a marine fuel and the first fully established integrated commercial green ammonia value chain from production to end use.[22] Ulsan was also the world’s first port to implement a green methanol bunkering system, and has begun supplying green methanol to ships.[23]

Driven by its 2050 carbon neutrality goals, South Korea is seeking alternative fuels such as hydrogen and ammonia to cut emissions from industry and power generation. As a result, in 2025, South Korea imported US$518 million of ammonia from Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, China, Australia, and Malaysia.[24]

Figure 2: Net Trade Balances in Hydrogen-Based Fuels and Commodities (2025)

Source: International Renewable Energy Agency[25]

Industrial collaboration between India and South Korea is also emerging in the green hydrogen and ammonia ecosystem. In 2025, South Korea’s KP Group partnered with AHES and India’s GH2 Solar to establish a 100,000 MTPA green ammonia project in India, combining Korean electrolyser technology with Indian renewable energy and manufacturing capabilities.[26]

Further, in March 2026, Reliance Industries and Samsung Construction and Trading (C&T) signed a 15-year agreement worth more than US$3 billion for the long-term supply of Indian green ammonia to South Korea. This creates one of the first largescale commercial linkages between India’s emerging green fuel production base and Korea’s industrial demand.[27] It builds on earlier investments, including the 2024 US$3 billion cooperation agreement between India’s ACME Group and Korea’s LTech UVC to develop green hydrogen and ammonia projects in India.[28]

Taken together, these developments point to a complementary bilateral value chain rather than parallel national transitions. India possesses the renewable resources, production potential, and port infrastructure to become a competitive supplier of green maritime fuels, while South Korea offers globally competitive capabilities in fuel-consuming vessels, bunkering technologies, and maritime engineering. Scaling cooperation across this production-to-consumption chain could form the foundation of an integrated India-Korea alternative maritime fuel ecosystem.

Green Ports as Integrated Energy Systems

Alternative fuels alone will not decarbonise maritime transport unless ports evolve alongside them. As shipping transitions away from conventional bunker fuels, ports are no longer simply logistics gateways but increasingly function as integrated energy systems that generate renewable electricity, electrify port operations, store and bunker low-carbon fuels, and digitally manage increasingly complex energy flows. The transition, therefore, extends well beyond vessel technology to the development of ports capable of simultaneously serving as renewable energy consumers, fuel production hubs, and clean energy distribution centres.

India has begun embedding this systems approach within its broader maritime decarbonisation strategy. The Harit Sagar Green Port Guidelines require major ports to progressively increase renewable energy use to more than 60 percent by 2030 and over 90 percent by 2047. It also mandates the simultaneous expansion of shore-toship power, electrifying cargo-handling equipment, deploying Electric Vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure, and establishing green hydrogen, ammonia and methanol bunkering facilities.[29] They also identify ports as future offshore wind support bases and require infrastructure development for green hydrogen storage and refuelling under the National Green Hydrogen Mission.

Implementation has already begun across several major ports. The VOC, Deendayal and Jawaharlal Nehru Ports are already operating predominantly on renewable electricity, while the Deendayal Port has begun generating surplus renewable power that can support future hydrogen production and port electrification.[30] The New Mangalore Port has achieved 100 percent solar power integration, while the Cochin Port plans to meet around 60 percent of its electricity demand through solar generation by 2030.[31]

Operational electrification is also progressing. At the VOC Port, ABB—a Swedish-Swiss technology company—has commissioned India’s first shore-to-ship power solution, enabling berthed vessels to switch off onboard diesel generators and draw electricity directly from the grid, massively reducing emissions and local air pollution during port stays.[32] The Mumbai Port is also introducing shore-to-ship power infrastructure, while Deendayal Port has deployed electric cargo-handling equipment in line with the Harit Sagar Guidelines.[33]

Under the Green Tug Transition Programme (GTTP), four major ports (Jawaharlal Nehru, Deendayal, Paradip, and VOC) will introduce battery-electric harbour tugs during the first implementation phase (2024–2027), before progressively adopting hydrogen, methanol, and ammonia-based propulsion technologies.[34]

At the same time, the Maritime Development Fund, with an allocation of approximately US$3 billion, is intended to support shipbuilding, green vessels, port infrastructure, and energy-efficiency investments, providing an important financing mechanism for India’s wider maritime energy transition with key timeline targets in 2030 and 2047.[35]

South Korea’s policy increasingly frames ports as integrated energy hubs where renewable power generation, energy storage, alternative fuel infrastructure, and digital optimisation operate as a single system. This approach is reflected in the International Shipping Decarbonization Promotion Strategy (2023), the Hydrogen Port Master Plan, and the Carbon Neutral Port Master Plan, which together promote renewable-powered port operations, expanded onshore power supply (OPS), alternative fuel infrastructure, and intelligent energy management.[36]

The electrification of port equipment without the decarbonisation of electricity supply merely shifts emissions from ports to the power sector, constituting what experts call “emissions externalization”.[37] This leads to a stronger emphasis on coupling port electrification with renewable energy deployment, distributed generation, and microgrids.

The Busan Port’s Global Hub Port strategy accordingly targets renewable electricity generation equivalent to 25 percent of port demand by 2032 and 100 percent by 2050, alongside expanded solar generation, offshore wind integration, fuel cells, and alternative marine power infrastructure.[38] In 2025, the Busan Port Authority launched the country’s first state-owned all-electric ferry−powered by ABB’s end-to-end electric propulsion system−as part of a national programme to replace 140 state-owned vessels with cleaner alternatives by 2030.[39]

Meanwhile, Incheon Port has established Korea’s first charging infrastructure for electrified cargo-handling equipment and is progressively electrifying yard tractors, forklifts, and other terminal machinery, while Busan Port Authority is integrating electricity demand forecasting, renewable energy planning, and digital energy management into future port expansion.[40]

Korea’s experience also reveals that the limitations of the wider energy system is a key factor that hinders port electrification. Although renewables accounted for 11.4 percent of national power generation by the end of 2025,[41] ports remain heavily dependent on the Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO) grid. Transmission bottlenecks and limited renewable energy access constrain deeper decarbonisation.[42] These challenges have reinforced policy attention towards renewable energy procurement, microgrids, distributed power systems and intelligent energy management. This positions ports not only as major electricity consumers but also as strategic renewable energy off-takers within the broader energy transition.

India’s comparative advantage lies in renewable electricity generation, land availability, and the expansion of new port infrastructure, while South Korea offers world-leading capabilities in port engineering, electrification technologies, digital energy management, and smart port operations. These capabilities, when integrated, suggest that future India-Korea cooperation should extend beyond individual technologies towards the joint development of integrated green port ecosystems capable of supporting both maritime decarbonisation and wider regional energy transitions.

From Complementarity to Partnership

Rather than viewing shipping, ports, and fuels as separate domains, both countries have an opportunity to jointly develop an integrated maritime energy ecosystem spanning fuel production, vessel technologies, port infrastructure, and regulatory frameworks. Existing institutional arrangements, including the India-ROK Comprehensive Framework for Partnership in Shipbuilding, Shipping and Maritime Logistics and the recent Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between India’s MoPSW and Korea’s Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, provide an institutional foundation for such cooperation.[43]

• Enhanced Cooperation on Joint Value-chain Development

Rather than pursuing isolated investments, both governments could work towards an India-Korea Green Maritime Energy Partnership centred on alternative maritime fuels and green port infrastructure. Existing commercial agreements, including the long-term Reliance Industries-Samsung C&T green ammonia supply agreement and emerging India-Korea hydrogen investments, demonstrate that industrial demand and commercial interest already exist.[44]

• Jointly Demonstrate Integrated Maritime Energy Systems

Beyond piloting hydrogen projects or bunkering facilities, India and Korea could jointly develop a demonstration green shipping corridor linking a major Indian port such as Deendayal or VOC with Busan or Ulsan around a common alternative fuel such as green ammonia or green methanol. Demonstration projects integrating renewable fuel production, bunkering infrastructure, alternative-fuel vessels, and port electrification would provide commercially valuable operational experience while helping reduce technology and investment risks. Such projects would also build on the growing emphasis on Green Shipping Corridors within both countries’ maritime strategies.[45]

• Scale Coordinated Finance, Standards, and Innovation

Financing remains one of the principal constraints to the large-scale deployment of maritime energy infrastructure. India’s Maritime Development Fund, together with financing from the Export-Import Bank of Korea (KEXIM), risk mitigation instruments from the Korea Trade Insurance Corporation (K-SURE), exportlinked financing from EXIM Bank India, investments from the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF), and multilateral institutions, such as the Asian Development Bank, Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and−where appropriate−the Green Climate Fund, could massively reduce investment risks for green port infrastructure, bunkering facilities, and alternative-fuel supply chains.

At the same time, cooperation should extend beyond financing to the alignment of fuel certification systems, bunkering protocols, and safety standards, while institutionalising collaboration through a bilateral Maritime Energy Innovation Platform bringing together ports, shipbuilders, fuel producers, equipment manufacturers, regulators, and research institutions. Existing industry linkages, including Korea Marine Equipment Association’s (KOMEA) Mumbai office and cooperation with Korea Marine Equipment Research Institute (KOMERI), provide an initial foundation on which such a platform could be built.[46]

Maritime decarbonisation is increasingly becoming an energy transition challenge rather than simply a shipping challenge, simultaneously requiring the development of renewable electricity, alternative fuels, green ports, and digitally integrated maritime infrastructure.

India and South Korea enter this transition from complementary positions: India offers scale in renewable energy, alternative maritime fuel production, and port expansion, while South Korea contributes technological leadership in shipbuilding, port engineering, and maritime digitalisation. If these complementary strengths are combined through coordinated industrial partnerships, demonstration projects, and aligned regulatory frameworks, the partnership could extend beyond bilateral cooperation to strengthen emerging green shipping corridors and resilient clean-energy supply chains across the Indo-Pacific. In doing so, India and South Korea would not only advance their own maritime decarbonisation objectives but also help shape the region’s transition towards a low-carbon maritime economy.

title: Marine biodiesel demand to more than double by 2031 without IMO framework – IEA
summary: The IEA projects marine biodiesel demand to double to 1.78 million tonnes by 2031, yet this "growth" would constitute a mere 0.6% of total marine fuel consumption, hardly a significant dent in carbon intensity. Driven primarily by FuelEU Maritime mandates, this minimal uptake suggests a glacial shift towards decarbonization, with actual alternative fuels and efficiency measures still severely lagging. While an IMO Net-Zero Framework could boost biodiesel use to 4% of total fuel, the industry's continued reliance on such marginal solutions underscores a systemic failure to address deep emissions cuts beyond token gestures.
content:
Global marine biodiesel demand will rise from just under 1 billion litres/year (around 890,000 mt/year) in 2025 to nearly 2 billion litres/year (around 1.78 million mt/year) by 2031, the International Energy Agency (IEA) forecasts.

That estimate assumes the IMO does not adopt its Net-Zero Framework, the global rules it has approved to cut GHG emissions from shipping.

Even so, marine biodiesel would make up only 0.6% of total marine fuel use by 2031, the IEA says.

It will remain the main source of renewable energy in shipping, but it will account for just 1% of the growth in renewable energy use across all transport.

Europe, where the FuelEU Maritime regulation is in place, will drive four-fifths of the growth. The IEA expects marine biodiesel to deliver much of the region’s near-term emission cuts while alternative fuels and energy efficiency measures are scaled up.

Most of the remaining increase will come from Singapore and China, where ports fuel vessels trading to Europe. Growth elsewhere will stay limited because of weak policy support.

FuelEU Maritime took effect at the start of 2025. It requires ships above 5,000 GT calling at EU ports to cut the GHG intensity of the energy they use. GHG intensity is measured well-to-wake and counts emissions from producing and distributing a fuel as well as burning it.

The required cut is 6% by 2030 and 14.5% by 2035. It covers all energy used on voyages within the EU and half of the energy used on voyages into or out of the bloc.

IMO framework would accelerate demand

The report says demand will climb much higher if the IMO adopts its Net-Zero Framework.

In that case, the IEA sees marine biodiesel use rising to more than 12 billion litres/year (more than 10.68 million mt/year) by 2031, or 4% of total marine fuel demand. A vote on the framework was pushed back from 2025 and is now due in December.

The framework would cover roughly 97% of the world’s merchant fleet by tonnage and set two tiers of targets for cutting the GHG intensity of ships’ fuel.

By 2030, ships would pay $100/mtCO2e for emissions above the tougher target of a 21% cut, rising to $380/mtCO2e for emissions above the base target of an 8% cut.

The IEA expects most ships to meet the 8% target by blending lower-emission fuels or buying credits, with marine biodiesel, liquefied natural gas (LNG) and liquefied biomethane (LBM) among the cheaper options available.

The 21% target would be harder to reach, as bio-methanol, e-methanol and ammonia remain scarce and costly, and the penalty for missing it is much lower, the report says.

The IEA assumes marine biodiesel supply would be enough for most ships to hit 8%, but not 21%, with competing road transport demand limiting supply.

title: Ahead of MEPC85, IMarEST members highlight barriers to Net-Zero delivery
summary: IMarEST members now cite "delivery, infrastructure, and value-chain coordination" as primary barriers to Net-Zero, a convenient deflection from concrete action. Despite theoretical confidence in decarbonisation pathways, the industry's investment remains stalled by uncertainties in fuel production and bunkering infrastructure. This ongoing inaction guarantees continued reliance on high-carbon fuels, setting the stage for escalating FuelEU Maritime fines and persistent emissions.
content:
Ahead of MEPC85, the Institute of Marine Engineering, Science and Technology (IMarEST) says its members now identify delivery, infrastructure, and value-chain coordination as the sector’s biggest barriers when it comes to IMO 2023 Greenhouse Gas strategy.

The Institute’s Ship Energy and Environment Special Interest Group (SEESIG) gathered views from professionals across ship management, classification societies, engineering, science, academia and maritime services.

They found little opposition to the IMO’s ambition of achieving Net-Zero emissions from international shipping. Instead, respondents overwhelmingly identified issues including infrastructure readiness, commercial incentives, fuel availability and the distribution of responsibility across the maritime value chain as the most significant barriers to the progress they are seeking.

Alasdair Wishart, director of technical and policy at the IMarEST commented: “We are not seeing opposition to the Net-Zero Framework, or to decarbonisation as a principle. This is extremely encouraging as the industry seeks clarity at MEPC85. In fact, our industry snapshot suggests that marine professionals are now increasingly focussing on whether the transition can be delivered at the pace required.”

Respondents expressed confidence in a range of potential decarbonisation pathways, including low and zero-carbon fuels, energy efficiency technologies, and operational improvements. However, many highlighted uncertainties around fuel production, bunkering infrastructure, supply chains and long-term regulatory frameworks as factors slowing investment decisions.

They also pointed to growing recognition that maritime decarbonisation cannot be delivered without increased collaboration in the industry. Participants highlighted the need for greater coordination between shipowners, operators, ports, fuel producers, charterers, cargo owners and policymakers to unlock emissions reductions across the sector.

Significantly, respondents identified operational measures such as voyage optimisation, digitalisation and just-in-time arrivals as among the most effective opportunities for reducing emissions in the near term. These findings suggest progress can be achieved today while longer-term fuel and propulsion solutions continue to scale.

Alasdair continued: “Shipping has a unique opportunity to take control of its emissions and accelerate the transition to Net-Zero. The cost of inaction is greater than the cost of action, and many of the technologies needed to reduce emissions already exist or are advancing rapidly.

“But we are seeing that the sector requires answers on how to create the conditions needed for investment confidence for fuels and infrastructure, as well as facilitation to kickstart collaboration on decarbonisation across the sector.”

title: Russia Takes Control of Two Chinese Heavy-Lift Ships Used for Arctic LNG 2 Deliveries
summary: Russia has quietly acquired two heavy-lift vessels, *Bright* (IMO 9830769) and *Glory* (IMO 9934498), to bolster its sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project logistics. These ships, now under Russian flag and Eco Shipping LLC, expand Moscow's opaque "shadow fleet" beyond oil and gas transport to critical project cargo. This move ensures the continued, carbon-intensive delivery of modules for a controversial energy project, all while evading transparent oversight.
content:
Russia has taken control of two modern heavy-lift carriers previously involved in transporting equipment for the sanctioned Arctic LNG 2 project, adding specialized project cargo vessels to an expanding network of shipping assets supporting the country’s Arctic energy ambitions.

The ownership change gives Moscow greater control over a critical part of the supply chain for its Arctic energy projects, from transporting construction modules to remote project sites to potentially delivering finished LNG infrastructure to future overseas customers. It also illustrates how Russia’s shadow fleet is evolving beyond the transportation of sanctioned oil and LNG into a more comprehensive logistics network supporting the entire lifecycle of its energy projects.

The vessels, Bright (IMO 9830769) and Glory (IMO 9934498), have reappeared on the Automatic Identification System (AIS) near Murmansk under the Russian flag, following changes in ownership and management to Russia’s Eco Shipping LLC, according to vessel records reviewed by gCaptain.

Equasis identifies Guangdong Nan Feng Shipping Co. as their previous owner. No information about the sale, its timing or financial terms has been made public. Neither vessel currently appears in the fleet listing on Eco Shipping’s website, although Equasis confirms the ownership changes.

The two vessels have a history of transporting oversized equipment for Arctic LNG 2. Glory previously sailed as Nan Feng Zhi Xing and Glory Ocean, while Bright has also operated under the names Zhi Xian Zhi Xing, Hunter Star and Bright Ocean. Both have been involved in transporting LNG project modules from China to Russia.

Earlier this year, the carriers delivered modules intended for the project’s third production train to Novatek’s LNG construction center at Belokamenka near Murmansk. In September, they returned to China and loaded two additional onshore power-generation (OPP) modules intended for the project’s second train.

The subsequent voyage to Arctic LNG 2 was conducted largely outside public tracking. The vessels switched off their AIS transponders while sailing north across the Pacific toward the Bering Strait in mid-September. They eventually delivered the modules to the Utrenniy terminal serving Arctic LNG 2 without broadcasting their positions. Both ships have since reappeared on AIS near Murmansk under their new Russian registration.

The future deployment of Bright and Glory remains unclear. At least seven additional modules intended for Arctic LNG 2’s third train remain in China, according to satellite imagery, with some appearing complete and others still under construction. The two carriers could potentially return to China to collect additional equipment.

Their new ownership could also open the door to other assignments supporting Russian LNG ambitions. Novatek has expressed interest in exporting its LNG technology and offshore platform concepts to international markets, including Africa and potentially Alaska. Heavy-lift carriers under Russian control could eventually transport modules from Belokamenka or other Russian facilities to overseas customers, rather than relying on foreign-owned vessels for such deliveries.

The development comes as two other Chinese heavy-lift carriers with connections to Russian Arctic shipping have attracted attention off Norway’s northern coast near Andøya.

One of them, Ya Qing Hai Yang, formerly known as Ocean 28, delivered a substation module from China to Arctic LNG 2 in 2024. The vessel, which encountered difficulties navigating ice-covered waters in the Chukchi Sea requiring assistance from Russian icebreakers and tugs, is sanctioned by the United States, European Union and United Kingdom.

The second vessel, Jian Yang Cheng He, has also been involved in voyages along the Northern Sea Route and has attracted scrutiny from Norwegian authorities. Norwegian authorities inspected both vessels after they appeared off the coast, with Ya Qing Hai Yang subsequently detained over deficiencies including an invalid flag registration and missing certificates.

The developments highlight how Russia’s shadow fleet is expanding beyond conventional oil tankers and LNG carriers. By bringing specialized heavy-lift vessels under domestic ownership and management, Moscow is gaining greater control over the transportation infrastructure required to sustain its Arctic energy projects, while reducing reliance on foreign-owned shipping companies.

The use of AIS-dark voyages has become a recurring feature of this trade, making independent monitoring of vessel movements and cargo deliveries considerably more difficult. Switching off AIS while navigating the Arctic is particularly concerning given the region’s remote operating environment and the importance of reliable vessel tracking for maritime safety.

Transparency surrounding Northern Sea Route operations has also deteriorated in recent years. Russian authorities no longer publish the daily operational shipping logs previously used to monitor traffic and have stopped making permit applications and granted permits publicly available.

title: The IMO NZF as agreed upon in 2025 still remains the most likely way to achieve the IMO 2023 GHG strategy
summary: As IMO Net Zero Framework negotiations intensify, analyses confirm that proposed compromises risk undermining genuine decarbonization efforts. Even slightly loosening Global Fuel Standard (GFI) trajectories directly translates to increased cumulative CO2 emissions, delaying urgent climate action. This political maneuvering highlights the industry's continuous push to soften environmental regulations, ensuring prolonged reliance on high-carbon fuels and deferring accountability.
content:
MEPC 85 is coming up fast, and negotiations for what the Net Zero Framework will look like are increasing in intensity. With several proposals on the table, it is likely that the outcome will be a composite, blending together different aspects of each proposal – although none of the new ideas have improved the entire regulation impact and the NZF as agreed upon in 2025 still remains clearly the most likely way to achieve the revised 2023 GHG strategy.

Any policy that is adopted needs to continue to support the IMO’s GHG goals. With each operational component of the NZF subject to separate negotiations, it is important to ensure the overall goals of the GHG Strategy are achieved.

UCL and Rocky Mountain Institute have conducted a sensitivity analysis on structural elements of the NZF, focusing on GFI trajectories and compliance prices (Remedial Units or Direct Contributions), as well as measuring the impact of differing ZNZ fuel reward schemes. This work has informed the recent Institute of Marine Engineering, Science & Technology (IMarEST) submissions (ISWG-GHG 23/2/9, 23/3/7, and 23/3/8 – see below). We have found (unsurprisingly) that higher ambition GFI trajectories with higher RU prices results in lower cumulative emissions. RMI/UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group modelling has clarified:

Even slightly loosening the GFI trajectory leads to higher cumulative emissions.

The GFI trajectory effectively sets the emissions allowed, making it one of if not the centerpiece of the entire policy; with negotiations considering loosening of the trajectory, there is possibility of undermining the entire purpose of the NZF as even slightly loosening the trajectory results in higher near-term emission while making later emission reduction more expensive and disruptive.

Lowering the price of Remedial Units leads to a rapid increase in cost of abatement and impact on states.

RUs can be seen as a measure of the incentivisation of investment in alternative energy: the higher the RU price, the stronger the investment in solutions that reduce emissions and therefore the lower the cost of abatement.

We tested the ‘as-is’ prices (RU1 = $100 and RU2 = $380) held constant, versus a scenario where the RU2 price starts at $380 increases over time (broadly reflecting the rising cost of emissions abatement as lower-cost measures are exhausted); only with RU price increasing was investment and energy transition sustained, leading to cost-effective emission reduction.

We also considered ‘No RU’ scenario reflected policy that only trades SUs for compliance, but included vessel impoundment as an enforcement mechanism. To represent the significant impact of impoundment, we modeled RU2 as $1,000 – showing that there is still an effective price on emissions in this policy design even if it is not labelled as such. Because the modelling assumes long-run equilibrium in prices, this policy still achieves emission reduction, but in practice the policy design creates high risks of disruption and high transport costs as volatility and price shocks in the energy system would be more directly translated into shipping price shocks than if there was a third compliance mechanism (RU price etc.)

The proposed ‘Direct Contributions’ are an alternative to RUs where shipping companies make payments to qualifying projects instead of paying the IMO; however, there is a possibility that companies will recover their contribution in the backend if they have financial stake in the project. We refer to this as ‘leakage’. We modeled this possibility by assuming an RU pricing scheme of 50/190, reflecting a 50% recovery of contributions. In every scenario, this led to substantially higher cumulative emissions than NZF ‘as is’, and much higher cost of abatement – as well as no IMO GHG fund for addressing JET.

ZNZ incentives of any kind must be differentiated by fuel type (e-fuels and biofuels) to achieve climate goals

Policies structured where incentives were not differentiated led to a massive increase in the use of biofuels and higher use of fossil fuels in the 2050 fuel mix compared to differentiated incentives.

Regional policies have included both rewards and multipliers successfully, but differentiate them to adjust to climate benefits and cost. For example, FuelEU utilizes multipliers, and the proposed ETS revision’s SMAP mechanism differentiates rewards by different proportions of each alternative fuel’s cost gap to conventional fuels.
